course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
unit.description: Compare additive and multiplicative change, then build, compose, invert, and model with exponential and logarithmic functions, including residuals and semi-log plots.

topic.title: Semi-log Plots
topic.summary: Semi-log plots with a logarithmically scaled y-axis, why exponential data appear linear on them, and the linear model log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a that comes from y = abˣ.

questions.prompt: A semi-log plot of a data set, with the y-axis logarithmically scaled, appears linear. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: A linear model is appropriate for the original data.
A logarithmic model is appropriate for the original data.
An exponential model is appropriate for the original data.
No model is appropriate, because the data were transformed.
questions.explanation: When the y-axis of a semi-log plot is logarithmically scaled, data that demonstrate exponential characteristics appear linear.
choiceExplanations: The semi-log plot is linear, not the original data.
A logarithmic model would appear linear if the x-axis were logarithmically scaled instead.
Linear on a y-semi-log plot means exponential.
Transforming data to test a model is exactly the purpose of a semi-log plot.
questions.distinguisher: The log is on y, so the original data are exponential.

questions.prompt: For y = 4(5)ˣ, which is the corresponding linear model on a semi-log plot with base 10?
choices: log y = (log 5)x + log 4
log y = (log 4)x + log 5
log y = 5x + 4
log y = (log 20)x
questions.explanation: For y = abˣ, the linear model is log_n y = (log_n b)x + log_n a. With a = 4 and b = 5: log y = (log 5)x + log 4.
choiceExplanations: Slope log b = log 5, intercept log a = log 4.
This switches the slope and the intercept.
The slope and intercept are logarithms of b and a, not b and a themselves.
a and b are not multiplied together before taking the logarithm.
questions.distinguisher: The base b gives the slope; the initial value a gives the intercept.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for the y-axis of a semi-log plot to be logarithmically scaled with base 10?
choices: Each unit on the y-axis represents adding 10 to the output.
The y-axis shows the output values divided by 10.
Both axes are scaled by powers of 10.
Each unit up represents multiplying the output by 10.
questions.explanation: On a logarithmic scale, each unit represents a multiplicative change of the base of the logarithm.
choiceExplanations: Adding 10 per unit is a standard scale.
Dividing by 10 rescales the axis but keeps it linear.
In a semi-log plot, only one axis is logarithmically scaled.
One unit up means one more factor of 10.
questions.distinguisher: Log scale: each unit is a factor, not an amount.

questions.prompt: A semi-log plot of exponential data, using base 10 on the y-axis, has the linear model log y = 0.5x + 1. Which exponential model matches?
questions.explanation: log a = 1 gives a = 10, and log b = 0.5 gives b = 10^0.5 ≈ 3.162. So y ≈ 10(3.162)ˣ.
choiceExplanations: The slope and intercept are logarithms; undo them with powers of 10.
The intercept 1 is log a, not a, and 0.5 is log b, not b.
This switches a and b.
questions.distinguisher: Intercept gives a = 10^(intercept); slope gives b = 10^(slope).

questions.prompt: For y = 6(1.5)ˣ, the semi-log plot uses the natural logarithm on the y-axis. What is the linear rate of change of the semi-log plot?
choices: ln 6
ln 1.5
log 1.5
questions.explanation: The linear rate of change is log_n b. With n = e and b = 1.5, it is ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405.
choiceExplanations: 1.5 is the base b, not its logarithm.
ln 6 is the initial linear value, log_n a.
Slope = ln b = ln 1.5.
log 1.5 uses base 10, but this semi-log plot uses the natural logarithm.
questions.distinguisher: The slope comes from the base, and it is a logarithm.

questions.prompt: Data values 3, 5, 9, 17, 33 are recorded at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. A semi-log plot of y is not linear for small x but becomes nearly linear for large x. Which statement is best supported?
choices: A transformation of an exponential function can model the data.
The data cannot be modeled by any exponential function.
A linear model is appropriate, because the plot becomes linear.
The semi-log plot must be wrong, because exponential data are always linear on it.
questions.explanation: If for large input values the logarithms of the outputs trend linear, transformations of an exponential function can be used to model the data. Here y − 1 = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, so y = 2^(x + 1) + 1.
choiceExplanations: y = 2^(x + 1) + 1, a transformation of an exponential function, fits the data.
A vertical translation of an exponential function still fits.
The semi-log plot trending linear points to an exponential model, not a linear one.
Only data of the form abˣ are exactly linear; translations trend linear for large inputs.
questions.distinguisher: Trending linear for large x still signals an exponential model.

questions.prompt: Why does taking the logarithm of y = abˣ produce a linear relationship in x?
choices: Because logarithms are always linear functions
Because the logarithm cancels the initial value a
Because exponential functions are linear for large x
Because log (abˣ) = log a + x log b
questions.explanation: The product property splits log (abˣ) into log a + log bˣ, and the power property turns log bˣ into x log b, a linear expression in x.
choiceExplanations: Logarithmic functions are not linear.
log a remains as the intercept; it is not canceled.
Exponential functions are never linear.
Product property, then power property, gives log a + x log b.
questions.distinguisher: The power property brings x down as a coefficient.

questions.prompt: On a semi-log plot with base 10 on the y-axis, a data point is plotted at (3, 2.5). What is the original output value at x = 3?
questions.explanation: The vertical coordinate is log y = 2.5, so y = 10^2.5 ≈ 316.228.
choiceExplanations: 2.5 is log y, not y.
12.182 ≈ e^2.5 uses base e instead of base 10.
0.398 ≈ log 2.5 takes another logarithm instead of undoing one.
questions.distinguisher: Undo the logarithm with a power of the base.

questions.prompt: A semi-log plot of data, using the natural logarithm, has a line through (0, 1.2) and (5, 3.2). Which exponential model matches the data?
questions.explanation: Slope = (3.2 − 1.2)/5 = 0.4 = ln b, so b = e^0.4. Intercept 1.2 = ln a, so a = e^1.2. y = e^1.2 (e^0.4)ˣ.
choiceExplanations: a = e^(intercept) and b = e^(slope).
The slope and intercept are natural logarithms of b and a.
There is no added constant; the plot is exactly linear.
This switches the roles of the slope and the intercept.
questions.distinguisher: Intercept gives a, slope gives b, both through e^(…).

questions.prompt: What is one advantage of semi-log plots for deciding whether an exponential model is appropriate?
choices: They make every data set, exponential or not, appear linear.
They remove the need to compute logarithms of the data.
They show the residuals of a model on the vertical axis.
Outputs need not be shifted by a constant to show the trend.
questions.explanation: An advantage of semi-log plots is that the dependent variable values do not need to be transformed by a constant to reveal that transformations of an exponential function would produce an appropriate model.
choiceExplanations: Only exponential data appear linear on a y-semi-log plot.
The vertical axis is a logarithm of the output.
A residual plot shows residuals; a semi-log plot shows the logarithms of the outputs.
This is the advantage the CED names.
questions.distinguisher: No need to subtract a constant first when looking for the trend.
